_: Nancy Rubins, 'Monochrome for Austin', 2015 — the largest work in the Landmarks collection, at the north-west corner of 24th and Speedway. Seventy aluminium canoes and small boats cantilevered off a stainless armature. EVERY number below carries the pixel or the publication it came from. See docs/real-art.md for the working.
name: Monochrome for Austin
atSource: landmarks.utexas.edu/artwork/monochrome-austin, 'GPS: 30.287462, -97.737132'. data/art.geojson's parts centre on -97.7370979, 30.2874649 (a buffered OSM node) — 3.4 m away. `atFromData` keeps the piece where its label and footprint already are.

dims.source: '600 x 642 x 492 inches' — landmarks.utexas.edu/artwork/monochrome-austin. 600 in = 15.24 m, 642 in = 16.31 m, 492 in = 12.50 m. scripts/bake_art.py's DIMS has the width at 15.85 m from a secondary source; 642 in off Landmarks' own object label is 16.31 m and is what this file uses.

hulls.countSource: 'a monumental sculpture consisting of 70 aluminum canoes and small boats' — landmarks.utexas.edu/artwork/monochrome-austin.
hulls.dimSource: MEASURED against the published height in Landmarks' elevation photograph (photo Paul Bardagjy, gallery image '29_rubins_monochromeforaustin'): the frame runs 750 px from the plinth's base to the topmost hull tip for the published 15.24 m, i.e. 49.2 px/m. Individual hulls measure 215-275 px long (4.4-5.6 m) and 35-42 px in the beam (0.71-0.85 m). Canoe and small-boat dimensions, which is what the object label says they are.
hulls.profileSource: As fractions of hull length: the keel rises 5.5% of length at the ends and the gunwale 10%, which is the pointed, up-swept canoe profile every hull in the photographs shows. A straight-sided slab is what the fill-extrusion bake had to draw and is the thing the owner called blocky.

cloud.envelopeSource: MEASURED in the same elevation photograph at 49.2 px/m: the mass runs from y=1100 px (its lowest hull, 2.4 m above grade, just clear of the plinth head) to y=505 px (15.24 m), so its centre sits 8.8 m up and its vertical semi-axis is 6.05 m; it spans 840 px = 17.1 m across that face against the published 16.31 m, so semiX 8.15 m. semiY is the published 12.50 m depth halved. `shell` biases sampling outward: 0 puts hull centres anywhere in the ellipsoid, 1 puts them all on its surface. 0.46 is what reproduces the photographs' open middle — the mass is a burst, not a lump.
cloud.radialSource: THE RULE THE OLD RECIPE MISSED, and it is the whole silhouette. In every photograph each hull's long axis points OUTWARD FROM THE CORE: the inner end is buried in the mass and the pointed end juts clear of it, so the work reads as a burst of boats. scripts/bake_art.py drew each hull at an INDEPENDENT random heading (`a = 2*pi*hash01('hull', ...)`), uncorrelated with where the hull sat, and an uncorrelated cloud of sticks is a lump however many of them there are. 0.82 is how far each hull is turned from its own random heading onto the radial one: 1.0 is a perfect sea urchin, 0 is the old bake.
cloud.spikesSource: Hulls placed on the envelope rather than sampled, because a sampled cloud almost never reaches its own outline — measured on the old bake, 32 random hulls came back 12.8 m wide against a published 15.85. The photographs are spiky: individual hulls jut a full length clear of the mass and those are what make the outline read as boats.

plinth.source: MEASURED in the elevation photograph at 49.2 px/m: the concrete pier is 40 px wide (0.81 m) and runs 115 px from grade to its head (2.34 m). It is strikingly small under a 16 m mass, and that contrast is most of why the work reads as cantilevered.

mast.source: The stainless yoke and armature stub above the plinth head, up into the underside of the cloud; 3.6 m is where the photographs' lowest hulls close over it. Mostly hidden by the time the cloud is drawn, which is correct — 'draws its support from a steel armature and intertwining cables' (Landmarks), and the armature is not what you see.

cables.source: 'intertwining cables' — Landmarks. A stainless cable on this piece is about 20 mm and would be sub-pixel at every zoom this app flies at, so it is DRAWN at 0.09 m: the same deliberate over-width as bake_tower.py's clock dial (3.05 m drawn for a true 3.66 m) and SLOPES_ROOFS.lines.ridge (1.0 m drawn for a true 0.4 m). The count is the number that reads against the sky in the elevation photograph, not a survey.

material.source: SAMPLED, and it corrects a real error. Median RGB of hull faces in Landmarks' photographs: lit #5e6166 and #77716f, shaded #423c3b, against a concrete plinth in the same frame at #cac2bc. The boats read at about HALF the luminance of concrete — weathered aluminium against a bright sky, not mill finish. scripts/bake_art.py painted them 'alum' #b9bec6 and 'mirror' #cdd8e0, which is a cloud of silver foil. Day is the diffuse reading brought onto the app's own concrete reference (js/props.js ARTMAT 'limest' #ded7c6 at 222 luma x 0.5). One hull in four takes the brighter tone, because the light-and-dark scatter across the mass is what makes seventy overlapping shells read as seventy objects rather than one.
material.plinthSource: SAMPLED off the plinth in the same photograph: (202,194,188).
material.steelSource: js/props.js ARTMAT 'steel', unchanged — the armature and cables keep the palette's own steel.
